notes.h: The Irish diet in the early twentieth century
notes.b: Before the mid-twentieth century most Irish households ate a simple diet based on home-grown and home-made foods. Knowing what people ate then, and why, is the starting point for judging how the diet has changed.
points: Potatoes were the staple food (the main food of the diet), eaten in large quantities with milk, butter and buttermilk. This made the diet high in starch.
Oatmeal (porridge) and home-baked wholemeal bread, such as soda bread and brown bread, supplied carbohydrate and fibre, so fibre intake was naturally high.
Vegetables were seasonal and home-grown, such as cabbage, turnips and carrots, while fresh fruit was limited. Eggs and fish were eaten where available, especially in coastal areas.
Meat, especially bacon and salted meat, was eaten occasionally rather than daily, so the diet was relatively low in fat and sugar.
The main meal, called dinner, was eaten at midday, and the family ate together at set times. Food was cooked from raw on an open fire or range.
Processed and convenience foods were largely absent, so meals were prepared from basic ingredients.
The diet was limited in variety, and poorer households could go short of food, so it was not simply 'healthy'.
A typical day's menu then: porridge or bread and tea for breakfast; potatoes, cabbage and bacon or fish for dinner at midday; bread, butter and tea in the evening.
notes.tip: Don't call the traditional diet simply healthy or unhealthy. Say it was high in fibre and low in fat and sugar, but limited in variety and sometimes inadequate.

notes.h: Changes in food and eating patterns since the early twentieth century
notes.b: Over the last hundred years the Irish diet has moved from basic, home-prepared food towards processed, imported and ready-made food. Each change affects nutrition, and each has reasons behind it.
points: Refined white flour and white bread replaced much of the wholemeal bread and oatmeal, which lowered the fibre content of the diet because refining removes the fibre-rich outer layers of the grain.
Rice and pasta partly replaced potatoes, and processed breakfast cereals replaced porridge for many families. The variety of foods and cooking methods increased.
Sugar, sweets, biscuits, cakes and soft drinks increased in the diet, adding empty kilocalories (energy with few nutrients). This made the diet more energy-dense and nutrient-poor.
Fat intake rose, from butter, cream, fatty meat, processed meat, cakes, pastries and fried foods.
Processed, frozen, canned and ready-made convenience foods became common, with microwave cooking, freezers and short preparation times, so fewer meals are prepared from raw ingredients.
Imported fruit and vegetables became available all year round, while home-grown seasonal produce declined. Supermarkets replaced local shops.
Eating out and takeaway meals became more frequent. Holidays abroad, immigration and television cooking introduced new dishes and ethnic foods.

Food labelling, health information and health campaigns gave consumers more knowledge of nutritional value, so low-fat, reduced-sugar, wholegrain, organic, vegetarian and special-diet products became widely available.
Reasons for the changes include rising incomes, urbanisation, women working outside the home, time pressures, food industry growth and advertising, refrigeration, supermarkets and education.
notes.tip: When asked for changes in the Irish diet, name the change and give its effect on nutrition or family life. Give reasons such as work patterns, income and availability; don't blame laziness.

notes.h: Contemporary trends in Irish eating patterns
notes.b: Today's eating patterns are shaped by busy lifestyles, convenience and growing health awareness. These trends are examined separately from the changes in the foods themselves.
points: Meals are irregular, and many people eat snacks and graze instead of eating planned meals. Meals, especially breakfast, are often skipped.
The main meal is often eaten in the evening rather than at midday, and family members may eat at different times, in front of the television or on the go.
Convenience and ready-made foods are chosen for speed, and microwave and barbecued foods form part of many diets.
Eating out and takeaways are a regular part of many households' diet.
Consumers show more health awareness, reading labels and choosing low-fat, low-sugar, organic, functional and plant-based foods, with allergen and special-diet products widely available.

Television, advertising, social media and food marketing influence food choices, particularly for children and teenagers. Busy work and study timetables, cost, food trends and celebrity chefs also play a part.
Concern for sustainability and locally produced food is growing.
Consequences include more obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease, linked to poor diet and inactivity, but also improved choice and food safety.
notes.tip: For trends in eating patterns, the points examiners look for include irregular meals, the main meal in the evening, family members eating at different times, and convenience foods. Say what each does to nutrition or family life.

notes.h: Comparing the Irish diet with current guidelines
notes.b: The Department of Health healthy eating guidelines and Food Pyramid are the benchmark for judging the Irish diet. Compared with them, the typical Irish diet is lower in fibre, fruit and vegetables, higher in saturated fat, and can be too high in salt and sugar.
points: Fibre: intake is below the guidelines because fewer wholegrain foods, fruit and vegetables are eaten.
Fruit and vegetables: intakes fall short of the five to seven portions a day recommended.
Saturated fat: intake is above the level recommended, from butter, fatty meat and processed foods.
Salt and sugar: intakes can be too high, especially from processed foods, sweets and drinks.
Fish: intake is lower than recommended, particularly oily fish. Many people also eat from the top shelf of the Food Pyramid (foods high in fat, sugar and salt) too often.
Iron and calcium: intakes are relatively low for some groups, especially teenage girls and women of child-bearing age.
Sugary drinks add empty kilocalories, and water is advised as the main drink.
Strengths of the Irish diet: widespread protein intake, the availability of lower-fat products, and a good milk and potato tradition.
notes.tip: In a comparison answer, identify the shortfalls against the guidelines and recommend corrections. Treat salt and sugar here only as part of the comparison, not as separate syllabus concerns.

notes.b: Low fibre is one of the four malnutrition concerns the syllabus names. Here malnutrition means an unbalanced diet, not only too little food. Write each concern as cause, effect and correction.
points: Cause: refining flour removes the bran and germ (the fibre-rich outer layers of the grain), so white bread and rice are low in fibre. Processed and convenience foods and few fruit and vegetables lower fibre, and wholegrain cereals are not eaten.
Effects: constipation, diverticular disease and other bowel disorders, and a higher risk of bowel cancer, because too little fibre slows the movement of waste through the bowel.
Fibre fills you up, so less fullness is linked to overeating and obesity. Low fibre is also linked to higher blood cholesterol and a raised risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

Corrective measures: choose wholemeal or wholegrain bread and pasta, oats or porridge, brown rice and high-fibre breakfast cereals. Eat fruit and vegetables with their skin where possible, add pulses such as beans and lentils, and use nuts and seeds.
Build up fibre gradually and drink plenty of fluid (water), so that the bowel is not upset.
The Irish Cancer Society gives information on diet, fibre and cancer risk.
notes.tip: For each concern, give cause, effect and correction in separate sentences, and link every fibre point to a disease.

notes.b: Too much saturated fat, the solid fat found mainly in animal foods and processed foods, is the second concern. It is linked to heart disease, so examiners expect effects as well as causes.
points: Sources: butter, cream, full-fat dairy, fatty and processed meats, pastries, cakes, biscuits, chocolate, fried and takeaway foods, and coconut and palm oil.
Causes: fast food and convenience foods, frying, snacking, large portions of fatty meat, and advertising.
Effects: raised blood cholesterol (LDL), which increases the risk of coronary heart disease and stroke. Excess energy from fat can lead to obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Corrective measures: use lower-fat milk, dairy and spreads, and choose lean meat. Grill, bake or steam instead of frying, and use unsaturated oils such as rapeseed or olive oil.
Replace some meat meals with oily fish, which supplies unsaturated fats. Limit the top shelf foods of the Food Pyramid and read labels.
The Irish Heart Foundation gives information on saturated fat, salt and heart health.
notes.tip: State cause, effect and correction in separate sentences, and link every fat point to a disease such as coronary heart disease.

notes.b: Iron is the third concern, and intakes are relatively low for some groups. Iron makes haemoglobin, so too little iron affects the whole body.
points: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the red pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body.
Sources: lean red meat, liver, eggs, wholegrain and fortified cereals, pulses, dark green vegetables and dried fruit.
Effects: iron-deficiency anaemia, with tiredness, pale skin, weakness and poor concentration. Headaches, breathlessness and poor resistance to infection can also occur.

Causes: low intake of red meat and iron-rich foods, the blood loss of menstruation, and rapid growth in adolescence, which increase the need for iron. Pregnancy, dieting and vegetarian diets without careful planning can also leave intake too low.
Tea and coffee with meals, and phytates (compounds in some plant foods), reduce iron absorption.

Corrective measures: include lean red meat, liver, eggs, wholegrain or fortified cereals, pulses and dark green vegetables. Eat foods rich in vitamin C, such as citrus fruit or fruit juice, at the same meal, because vitamin C improves iron absorption.
Avoid tea with meals, and take supplements only on medical advice.
notes.tip: Iron-deficiency anaemia is the effect the marking schemes look for, though it is not the only one. Name the groups at risk, such as teenage girls and women of child-bearing age.

notes.b: Calcium is the fourth concern. It does several jobs in the body, so low intake has effects on bones, teeth, muscles and blood.
points: Calcium is needed for the formation of bones and teeth, blood clotting, muscle contraction and normal nerve function.
Sources: milk, yoghurt, cheese, fortified plant milks, dark green vegetables, nuts and seeds such as sesame seeds, and fish eaten with its bones, such as sardines.
Effects: poor bone growth in children, weak bones and osteoporosis (brittle bones) in later life, dental decay, muscle cramps, and slow or impaired blood clotting.

Causes: low intake of milk, yoghurt and cheese (through dieting, dislike, cost, or replacement by soft drinks), and low vitamin D, which is needed to absorb calcium. Poor sunlight and little oily fish lower vitamin D.

Corrective measures: have three servings a day of milk, yoghurt and cheese (lower fat) or fortified plant alternatives. Eat fish with edible bones, dark green vegetables, nuts and seeds, and add fortified foods.
Get vitamin D from oily fish, eggs and safe sunlight, and do weight-bearing exercise. Take supplements only on medical advice.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for the effects of calcium deficiency and for its sources and functions. Give effects such as osteoporosis, dental decay, muscle cramps and slow clotting.

notes.h: Method: comparing a day's menu with the guidelines
notes.b: A common activity is to compare a typical day's menu from the start of the twentieth century with one from today. The same five steps work for any menu.
points: Step 1: list every food and drink eaten in the day, with portion sizes.
Step 2: identify the sources of fibre, saturated fat, salt, sugar, iron and calcium in the menu.
Step 3: compare each nutrient with the healthy eating guidelines, saying whether it is too high, too low or about right.
Step 4: recommend specific changes, such as wholegrain instead of white bread, a serving of fish, or a lower-fat dairy choice.
Step 5: rewrite one meal or the whole day to show the changes.
notes.tip: Make recommendations specific, naming the food and the swap, rather than saying 'eat more healthily'.

notes.h: Method: reading data on Irish consumption
notes.b: Section B often has a data question on Irish food consumption or the Food Pyramid. A fixed routine lets you pick up the marks for reading, describing, explaining and recommending.
points: Read the title, the units, the years covered and the groups surveyed before drawing conclusions.

Identify the trend by comparing the first and last data points, noting a rise, a fall or a small change, and any change of direction in between. Compare groups too, such as men and women or age groups.
Quote the figures from the data exactly, and state which food or nutrient they describe.
Compare the data with the healthy eating guidelines and link the difference to a health risk such as heart disease, obesity or anaemia.
Suggest a reason for the trend, such as convenience foods, eating out, advertising, income or changes in family routines, and finish with a recommendation.
notes.tip: Data questions ask you to describe trends, give reasons, comment on health consequences and recommend change. Use only the figures printed in the question.

keyTerms.definition: Poor nutrition caused by a diet that is unbalanced, supplying too much or too little of one or more nutrients.
A fat, mainly from animal foods, that raises blood cholesterol when eaten in excess.
Indigestible plant material in wholegrain foods, fruit and vegetables that aids bowel function.
Flour from which the bran and germ have been removed, lowering its fibre and nutrient content.
The red pigment in blood that carries oxygen, which contains iron.
A condition of tiredness and weakness caused by too little iron to make enough haemoglobin.
A condition in which bones become weak and brittle, often caused by long-term low calcium intake.
A ready-made or quick-to-prepare food that saves time in cooking.

factCards.definition: Irregular meals and snacking; main meal eaten in the evening; more eating out; more convenience and microwave foods.

questions.prompt: Outline two changes in the Irish diet since the early twentieth century.
questions.model: Refined white flour and white bread replaced wholemeal bread and oatmeal, lowering fibre intake. Rice and pasta partly replaced potatoes, and sugar, fat and processed convenience foods increased, with more eating out and takeaway meals. Full marks need a clearly stated change and a brief explanation of its effect on nutrition or eating pattern.

questions.prompt: Discuss the malnutrition concerns in the current Irish diet, with reference to the causes, effects and corrective measures for a low iron intake.
questions.model: Concerns: low dietary fibre, high saturated fat, relatively low iron and calcium. Iron: needed for haemoglobin, which carries oxygen; low intake causes iron-deficiency anaemia, with tiredness, pale skin, weakness and poor concentration. Causes: low intake of red meat, menstrual blood loss and the growth of adolescence, plus convenience foods and irregular meals replacing iron-rich home cooking. Corrective measures: lean red meat, wholegrain or fortified cereals and pulses, eaten with vitamin C foods to improve absorption. Any answer should set iron against the healthy eating guidelines and relate the low intake to the eating patterns of the early twentieth century and today.
